question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The opening that is normally quoted in the theory literature is the i – v opening of Eleanor Rigby.

The piece is in E minor. The string quartet intro is laid out

E minor – B minor – …

i = E minor is the tonic of the piece and the chord that follows it is the
minor fifth-degree chord of the key, v = B minor, the chord whose root is a
perfect fifth above the tonic. In the classic i–v lament form that is the
first two-chord jump you hear, E–B, tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord,
before the progression goes on to G major and so on. 

The same i–v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening is the one that is most often
cited for the Beatles’ minor-key instrumentals, e.g. Yer Blues / In My
Life etc., in E minor the textbook i–v is the E minor – B minor opening of
Eleanor Rigby. That is the tritone-free minor-fifth-degree jump that is
meant by a tonic → v jump.

If the jump is taken in the strict interval sense I → ♭V, a tritone/root-a-
minor-fifth jump, the classic Beatles tritone intro quoted in the literature
is the C-major → G♯/Ab major/minor colouring that opens Come Together /
I Am The Walrus, the Beatles’ best-known tonic-to-flat-five, tonic-to-minor-
fifth-interval, opening.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example that is usually quoted is *A Hard Day’s Night*.

The verse is in G major. The very first harmonic gesture that you hear on the guitar is the tonic G major – the famous “A Hard Day’s Night’’ G6/ G7 colour – and it is answered immediately by the minor v, D minor, G → Dm, i.e. a perfect-fifth / fourth jump up from the tonic to the chord built on the fifth degree of the major scale, which in a major key is normally minor. It is the I → v opening that gives the song its characteristic lift.

The same I → v gesture is the one that is most often cited for the early mid-’60s E-major material, e.g. *Ticket to Ride / Can’t Buy Me Love* in E major E → Bm, i.e. I → v in E, the formal prototype of the A Hard Day’s Night opening.

The textbook tonic → minor-fifth-degree opening is the minor-key i – v, and the Beatles canonical example of that is Eleanor Rigby.

The piece is in E minor. The string quartet intro is heard as

E minor – B minor – ...

i = E minor is the tonic of the piece. The chord that immediately follows it is the chord built on the 5th degree of E minor, B–D–F♯, i.e. v. In natural minor the fifth-degree chord is minor, so the opening is a clear perfect-fifth up root move E → B from tonic to the minor v chord before the progression continues to G major etc. That i–v lament opening is the one consistently cited in theory literature for the Beatles minor-key instrumentals.

A Hard Day’s Night is an I–v gesture in the literature, but the actual first harmonic gesture of the song is not a clean G → Dm jump. The famous opening colour is the G6/Gadd9 voicing that is heard over the whole introductory riff, and the functional harmony of the verse is I–IV–I–V in G major, G – C – G – D. The E-major I–v prototype Colleague 2 mentions for Ticket to Ride / Can’t Buy Me Love is a verse-level description rather than the literal first two chords heard at the outset, whereas Eleanor Rigby’s E minor – B minor is literally the first two chords you hear.

If the question is taken in the strict interval sense tonic → ♭V, i.e. a root tritone / minor-fifth interval up, the Beatles best-known example is the C major → G♯/A♭ colour that opens Come Together / I Am The Walrus. That is a different reading of “minor fifth” than tonic → v.

On the usual tonic → minor-quality fifth-degree reading, Eleanor Rigby is the clearest and most often quoted Beatles opening.
